landmark_cases.title: In re E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co.
landmark_cases.reason: Establishes the thirteen-factor framework for assessing likelihood of confusion under Lanham Act § 2(d), which governs the TTAB’s analysis and the Federal Circuit’s review.

landmark_cases.title: Juice Generation, Inc. v. GS Enterprises LLC
landmark_cases.reason: Explains how a considerable number of third-party uses/registrations of a common term can show a crowded field and reduced mark strength, central to DuPont factor six and commercial impression.

landmark_cases.title: Jack Wolfskin Ausrüstung für Draussen GmbH & Co. KGaA v. New Millennium Sports, S.L.U.
landmark_cases.reason: Further develops the ‘crowded field’ doctrine: voluminous third-party use/registration evidence can demonstrate weakness and narrow scope of protection, affecting the sixth and first DuPont factors.

landmark_cases.title: Coach Services, Inc. v. Triumph Learning LLC
landmark_cases.reason: Addresses how to evaluate relatedness/similarity of services and the role of third-party registrations in showing that goods/services may emanate from a single source, key to DuPont factor two.

landmark_cases.title: Palm Bay Imports, Inc. v. Veuve Clicquot Ponsardin Maison Fondee En 1772
landmark_cases.reason: Confirms that evidence of third-party use of similar marks on similar goods indicates a weaker mark entitled to a narrower scope of protection, guiding factor six.

landmark_cases.title: Olde Tyme Foods, Inc. v. Roundy’s, Inc.
landmark_cases.reason: Clarifies that ‘similar’ goods/services—not identical ones—suffice in the DuPont analysis, relevant to maintaining a consistent similarity scope across factors (including factor six).
